_note: 2026-09-06. The interpreter-deletion hole in command_rules.tool_discipline/delete-outside-disposable, and the __pycache__ allowlist decision taken with it. Every case here runs through the SAME rule (there is no second rule and no second allowlist) -- see config.json _note_interpreter_delete for the line drawn and what deliberately falls outside it. `parity: false` on the blocking cases with no `parity_exception`: there is no .ps1 master to diverge FROM, the pattern additions post-date the cutover entirely, and CONTRACT-ARCHIVE.md's §7 table is not this task's to edit.
THE EXACT BYPASS AS REPORTED, in its second natural spelling. os.remove is what an agent reaches for when the target is a file rather than a tree.
`python -c` is not the only spelling: node -e reaches exactly the same place, and rmSync/unlinkSync are matched via the (sync)? suffix rather than as separate names.
A heredoc piped to an interpreter: the delete call is on its own LINE, which segment_split_pattern already splits on, and detect_pattern spans the newline via [\s\S]{0,600}?.

MUST-NOT-BECOME-A-BLANKET-BAN, half 1: the identical one-liner against a path INSIDE the disposable allowlist is still permitted. If this flips to 2 the rule has become 'interpreters are forbidden', which would be switched off by the first user who hit it.

MUST-NOT-BECOME-A-BLANKET-BAN, half 2: THE PROJECT'S OWN TEST INVOCATION -- the shape that would break first, and the one the brief named. It carries an interpreter and a path but no deletion call, so detect_pattern never fires.
The false-positive case the generic token_reject qualifier exists for: `.remove(` on an ordinary Python object is not a filesystem call, and `a.remove` must not be reported as a path.

INVARIANT: the owner-grant path still works, and now works through the interpreter form too -- the same pm-delete-allow ledger, the same main-chain requirement, the same consumption. Same setup schema as r3-14.
__pycache__ DECISION, half 1: the routine need that produced the incident is now simply allowed, by rm and by interpreter alike.

__pycache__ DECISION, half 2 -- THE PATTERN CANNOT BE WIDENED BY A PATH THAT MERELY CONTAINS THE SUBSTRING. Both alternatives are bounded at each end; these two are the shapes an unbounded `__pycache__|\.pyc` would have waved through.

2026-09-06 M1. A QUOTED SHELL WRAPPER was not a segment start, so the delete verb inside it was never looked at. `bash -c` is the plainest spelling and the one an agent reaches for after `rm -rf` is refused.
Single quotes, `sh` rather than `bash`: the wrapper list is a word alternation, so both spellings have to hold or only one was fixed.

THE ONE THAT MATTERED MOST: `powershell -Command "Remove-Item ..."` is the NATIVE Windows spelling, and the rule's own block message names Remove-Item as covered. It was not. A message that promises what the rule does not do is worse than no message.
cmd /c, the last of the four wrapper spellings.
NOT A BLANKET BAN ON WRAPPERS: the same wrapper deleting inside a disposable location still runs, through the SAME allowlist as a bare `rm`.

THE FALSE POSITIVE THAT DECIDED THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. A quoted delete verb ALONE was tried first and turned this ordinary commit into a block; requiring a WRAPPER WORD near the verb is what keeps it allowed. A rule that blocks routine work gets switched off, and then protects nobody.
Same false-positive class, second verb: `del` followed by a path-shaped token inside a commit message.
A wrapper with no deletion in it is untouched -- detect_pattern never fires, so nothing downstream runs.

RESIDUE, PINNED AS ALLOWED SO IT IS NOT MISTAKEN FOR COVERAGE, and NARROWED in round 2 to what it actually is: piped deletion where the path is in the OTHER segment. Here the literal path is `echo`'s argument and the verb comes after the pipe, so no single segment holds both and the token check has nothing to judge -- that half is out of reach of a segment-based rule by construction. What round 2 CLOSED is the case this note used to be read as covering: `xargs` IS a wrapper word now, so `echo x | xargs rm -rf <literal path>` and `xargs -I{} rm -rf <literal path>` block (td-int-49, td-int-50), because there the verb and the literal path DO share a segment. See config.json _note_interpreter_delete (e).

THE SECOND FALSE POSITIVE, and the reason the wrapper alternative is ANCHORED at segment start rather than matched anywhere. `bash`, `sh` and `cmd` are ordinary English words in a commit message, and an unanchored wrapper word within 120 characters of a delete verb turned this into a block. See config.json _note_interpreter_delete.

2026-09-06 FINAL REVIEW, second sweep. Seven more spellings measured ALLOWED through the dispatcher, all of them what an agent reaches for the moment `rm -rf` is refused -- so by this rule's own standard (a spelling a writer produces naturally is the rule not working) they are defects, not residue. Cases 28-35 are those seven plus the second `find` form; 36-42 are the false positives that shape the fix, re-run; 43-44 pin what is still open. See config.json _note_interpreter_delete, final paragraph.
An ABSOLUTE-PATH invocation of the verb. Closed by an optional path prefix that must end in a separator, which is why `git rm` and `cp a/rm b` below are unaffected.
The same three INSIDE M1's own wrapper form. The wrapper branch required the verb immediately after the quote, so a prefix word between the two walked straight past it -- M1's scope, missed by M1.
`find -delete` carries no shell delete VERB at all, so neither pattern had anything to match. A `find` branch in both closes it; the directory argument is the path token judged.
`find -exec rm`: `\;` splits the command, and the surviving segment starts with `find` rather than with the verb, so the verb branch never saw it.

THE FALSE POSITIVE THE PREFIX RULE IS SHAPED AROUND: `git rm` is ordinary tracked-file work that git itself records, and `git` must never join the prefix-word list. The prefix must END in a separator, which is what keeps this allowed.
Same rule, other direction: a path whose BASENAME is the verb is not a verb invocation, because the segment does not start with it.
The commit-message false positive for the NEW prefix words, the fourth of its family. `sudo` and `env` are ordinary English near a delete verb; segment-start anchoring is what keeps this allowed.

Searching the source for the `find` form must not be the `find` form. The detect branch fires here; the segment starts with `grep`, so nothing blocks -- the same two-stage absorption every other quoted mention relies on.
NOT A BAN ON THE PREFIX WORDS THEMSELVES: `sudo` and `env` with no delete verb after them are ordinary invocations and detect_pattern never fires.

RESIDUE, PINNED AS ALLOWED SO IT IS NOT MISTAKEN FOR COVERAGE, and PRE-EXISTING rather than introduced by the `find` branch: a target with no separator and no dot is not a path-shaped token, so the token check has nothing to judge -- `rm -rf owner-files` has always been allowed and `find owner-files -delete` inherits it exactly. Widening path_token_pattern to bare words would make every flag and subcommand a candidate path.

WHAT THE `find` BRANCH COSTS, pinned so the trade is visible rather than discovered: `find . -name '*.pyc' -delete` now BLOCKS on the `.` token, exactly as `rm -rf .` always has. It is a recursive delete rooted at cwd, not at a disposable directory, so blocking is the safe direction -- and the routine bytecode path an agent actually needs, `rm -rf <dir>/__pycache__`, stays allowed by the allowlist, which is what keeps this from manufacturing the incentive to route around the rule. See td-int-45 for the other, more common half of the same trade.

THE SECOND AND MORE COMMON COST OF THE `find` BRANCH, pinned so it is disclosed rather than discovered: `-name`'s argument is a path-shaped token like any other, so this blocks on `*.map` even though `dist/` IS allowlisted. Rejecting `*`-leading tokens would allow `rm -rf *.db`, which is a real hole traded for a cosmetic one, so it was not done. The escape hatch is the shell glob -- `rm -rf dist/*.map` is allowed, because there the token carries its directory (td-int-46).
The escape hatch named in td-int-45, pinned as ALLOWED so a later change cannot close both at once and leave disposable deletes with no spelling at all.

2026-09-06 final review round 2. THE RESIDUE CLAIM THAT WAS FALSE. docs/DESIGN.md said quote nesting 'over-blocks, never under-blocks'; a quoted verb AT SEGMENT START under-blocked -- measured rc=0. It is a spelling an agent types straight after a block. Closed by an optional quote around the verb in both patterns; the false positive that shaped the ORIGINAL fix (a quoted verb ANYWHERE, td-int-23) stays allowed because this alternative is still anchored at segment start.

THE SECOND FALSE RESIDUE CLAIM. `xargs` was called out of reach 'by construction' -- true only when the path is in another segment. With `-I{}` the literal path is right there in the xargs segment, so the verb and the path DO meet. `xargs` is a wrapper word now; td-int-26 still pins the genuinely-out-of-reach half.
LOW, closed in passing with the two above: four more prefix words an agent reaches for, each measured rc=0 first.
FALSE-POSITIVE RE-RUN for the widened wrapper list. `docker rm` is a subcommand, not a shell delete: `docker` is not a wrapper word, so the segment does not start with a delete verb.

tool_input.command: gh pr comment --body "we should rm dist/"

_note: The new prefix words are not banned, only watched: with no delete verb after them detect_pattern never fires.
Searching the source for a blocked spelling must not be the blocked spelling: the segment starts with `grep`.

2026-09-06 round 3. THE WRAPPER BRANCH SWALLOWED INTERVENING WORDS: `[^"']{0,120}` between the wrapper word and the verb matched ANY text, so a wrapper in front of a NON-shell `rm` subcommand became a false block while the unwrapped form was allowed. The option run is now explicit -- flags (`-x`, `--long`, `/c`) and a bare number (for `timeout 5` / `nice -n 10`) -- so the verb has to be the first word after it, exactly the way the sudo|env|exec prefix run already worked.

`env FOO=1 npm rm ./pkg` stays ALLOWED, but as of round 4 for a different reason than this note first gave: `VAR=value` IS part of the option run now (td-int-77 needs it), so the run consumes `FOO=1` and stops at `npm` -- which is not a delete verb. `env rm -rf <path>` (td-int-29) still blocks: no option run at all, verb first.
The other half of the same fix: a NUMBER is part of the option run, so `timeout <n> rm` is still the wrapped delete it always was.
MEDIUM-2: three more wrapper words an agent reaches for straight after a block, each measured rc=0 first. The list is an ENUMERATION and cannot be completed -- see td-int-73 for the pinned residue.

RESIDUE, PINNED AS ALLOWED SO THE ENUMERATION IS VISIBLE: the wrapper set is a LIST OF WORDS, so any prefix command not on it passes. `setsid`, `stdbuf -o0`, `watch -n1`, `ionice` all measured rc=0 and are not closable by adding three more names -- the next one is always unlisted. Adding a name is cheap when a real spelling shows up; pretending the set is complete is what this fixture prevents. See config.json _note_interpreter_delete and docs/DESIGN.md.

2026-09-06 round 4. THE OPTION RUN STOPPED AT AN OPTION'S ARGUMENT: `-u` matched, `root` did not, so the run ended and the verb was no longer 'next' -- the segment was skipped and the delete ran. An option may now carry ONE non-flag argument. The false-positive half is td-int-78: the argument is consumed, not treated as a verb.
`VAR=value` is its own alternative in the option run: it is how `env` is actually used, and without it `env VAR=1 rm -rf <path>` walked past.
THE FALSE POSITIVE THE ARGUMENT RULE IS SHAPED AROUND: consuming an option's argument must not make the NEXT word a verb. `npm` is not a delete verb, so this is untouched.

ROUND 4, and it was a real defect rather than the 'noise' an earlier note called it: the prefixed verb `/usr/bin/rm` is itself path-shaped, so it became a bad path and BLOCKED a delete the allowlist PERMITS -- `rm -rf dist/x` was allowed and the same delete spelled with an absolute verb was not. A rule that refuses permitted work is the failure mode this whole rule is organised against. The verb token is rejected now, with or without a directory prefix. RESIDUE, accepted knowingly and in the same family as the pre-existing `foo.rm` one: a file whose basename IS a delete verb (`rm -rf tools/rm`) is no longer judged, so deleting it is allowed.

The same defect in its native Windows spelling: `/s` and `/q` are switches, not paths, and they were being reported as bad paths for a delete inside `dist/`. Single-letter `/x` tokens are rejected now. RESIDUE: an absolute POSIX path one character long (`/s`) is no longer judged either.

RESIDUE, PINNED AS A BLOCK BECAUSE THAT IS WHAT IT DOES: a `|` INSIDE A QUOTED STRING is still a segment separator, so this splits and the second half starts with `/usr/bin/rm"` -- a verb at segment start with a path after it. Reported in round 4 as if it were the token issue above; it is not. Without the pipe the identical command is rc=0 (the round-4 verb-token fix), and this is the SAME pre-existing class as `git commit -m "x; rm docs/old.md"` (td-int note in config.json): the segment splitter has no notion of quoting, and that is the segment-extraction rework, not a pattern widening.

RESIDUE, PINNED: the verb set contains two-letter words that are whole commands elsewhere. `ri` is Ruby's documentation browser and `rd` is a directory-removal builtin; `ri lib/foo.rb` reads a file and is blocked as if it deleted one. Not cheaply fixable -- dropping `ri`/`rd` from the verb set would open the PowerShell and cmd spellings the set exists for -- so it is named here rather than left to be met.

RESIDUE, PINNED AS ALLOWED: the price of the round-4 verb-token exclusion. The token reject that stops `/usr/bin/rm` being reported as a bad path is spelled `([^\\s]*[\\\\/])?(verb)(\\.exe)?`, so it also drops any path whose BASENAME is a delete verb -- `tools/rm`, `tools/rm.exe`, `src/del`. Deleting one of those is no longer judged. Accepted because the alternative was measured worse: without the exclusion the rule BLOCKED `/usr/bin/rm -rf dist/x`, a delete its own allowlist permits, and a rule that refuses permitted work is the failure mode this rule is organised against. Same family as the pre-existing `foo.rm` residue and the single-letter `/s` switch.
